passage:
Dear diary, Wednesday
Best lunch break ever. I told everyone about the new laptop Abbu is getting me, and the holiday abroad in May, five-star hotel, pool on the roof. Everyone went quiet, which means they were impressed. I also mentioned that the tuition teacher says I'm the smartest in the batch.
Keerthana rolled her eyes at the hotel part. Probably jealous. Then she sat with the 9B girls for the rest of lunch and didn't save me a seat on the bus. Weird. Maybe her stomach was upset.
Tomorrow I'll tell them about the concert tickets. That should get them talking again.
Honestly, though, nobody asked me anything today. They just said "nice" and looked at their phones.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Sabina say about the hotel?
qa.a: Sabina said it was five-star, with a pool on the roof.

qa.q: What does Sabina think the quiet at lunch means, and what might it really show?
qa.a: Sabina thinks it means everyone was impressed, but it may show boredom or unease, since nobody asked anything and they looked at their phones.

qa.q: What could Sabina try at tomorrow's lunch instead of talking about the concert tickets?
qa.a: Sabina could ask the others about their own week and really listen, which might bring Keerthana back more than another boast.

qa.q: How might Keerthana be feeling about Sabina's stories?
qa.a: Keerthana seems tired of the bragging; her rolled eyes and choosing the 9B table suggest she is quietly pulling away.

grounding: A teenager boasts about money and status to rank higher with the group, and misses the rolled eyes and quiet distancing around Sabina.

qa.q: What did Zainab say about the new flat?

grounding: A teenager's bragging in a group chat about possessions and status leaves others quiet, and a friend points out what Zainab had not noticed.

passage:
After school, the boys and girls of the kasba gathered at Bhola's tea stall by the bus stand, and Samir, as usual, did most of the talking.
"My chacha sent money from the Gulf again," he said, flashing a new phone. "Big amount. Next month, a bike."
Pooja, sitting on the bench with her geography notes, glanced at the others. One boy rolled his eyes. Another suddenly remembered he had to fetch milk.
"You should see our new fridge," Samir went on. "Double door. Nobody in this whole town has one."
Pooja closed her notebook. "We've heard about the fridge, Samir."
He laughed and kept going, now about his cousin's car. He didn't see the two girls from his class quietly pick up their bags and walk toward the temple road. By the time his tea was finished, only Pooja was left, and she was only waiting for her bus.

qa.q: What did Samir say his chacha sent from the Gulf?
qa.a: He said his chacha sent money from the Gulf again.

qa.q: Why might Samir keep talking about money and the fridge?
qa.a: Samir seems to feel that showing off possessions will make the group admire him and rank him higher, and he is eager for that approval.

qa.q: What could Samir notice or try to keep his friends close?
qa.a: He could notice who leaves while he talks, and ask the others about their own day instead of listing what his family owns.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Samir's bragging?
qa.a: Pooja finds it tiring and repetitive, which is why she reminds him they've heard about the fridge and only stays for her bus.

grounding: It shows a teenager talking up money to rise in the group while others roll their eyes and quietly leave, which he fails to notice.

passage:
At the lunch tables of the secondary school in Porto, Pablo was telling the story again.
"So this guy at the skate park shoves my friend, right? And I just walk up and tell him, 'Try that with me.' He backs off. Three of his friends too."
Last week it had been two friends. The week before, one.
The younger boys at the table leaned in. Priscila, who had been Pablo's friend since primary school, kept eating her soup. She had been at the skate park that day. What she remembered was Pablo saying "sorry" and pulling his friend away fast.
"You should have seen his face," Pablo said, louder.
Priscila picked up her tray and moved to the table by the window, where her lab partners were arguing about homework. Pablo didn't look up. He was already starting on the fight at the football pitch.

qa.q: How many of the other boy's friends backed off in this week's version?
qa.a: Three of his friends too.

qa.q: What might Pablo want when he tells the fight story louder?
qa.a: Pablo probably wants the younger boys to be impressed and to see him as tough, and he feels good when they lean in.

qa.q: What went wrong for Pablo, and what could help?
qa.a: His stretched fight stories pushed away a real friend; telling what actually happened and noticing who leaves could keep his friendships.

qa.q: How does Priscila feel about the fight story?
qa.a: Priscila feels uncomfortable and a little distant, because she remembers Pablo saying sorry, so she quietly moves to another table.

grounding: It shows a teenager inflating fight stories to rank higher in the group while an old friend quietly distances herself, unnoticed.

passage:
In the girls' wing of the district sports hostel, lights-out was at ten, and Vasudha always saved her best stories for nine-thirty.
"At my old school, a senior tried to take my place in the kabaddi team. I told her in front of everyone, 'Take it if you can.' She cried in the changing room. After that, nobody touched my things."
The girls on the lower bunks laughed. Charu, her roommate, lay facing the wall.
Charu had heard three versions of this story in two weeks. In one, the senior had cried. In another, she had left the school. Every night the stories got harder and louder, and every night Vasudha checked everyone's faces.
The next morning, Charu asked the warden if she could swap rooms with a girl from the athletics group. She didn't give a reason.
Vasudha only found out when she saw the new name on the door.

qa.q: What time was lights-out in the girls' wing?
qa.a: Lights-out was at ten.

qa.q: What does Vasudha checking everyone's faces suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Vasudha feels anxious for approval and wants the group to see her as tough and important.

qa.q: What small step could help Vasudha make real friends in the hostel?
qa.a: She could share an ordinary true story or ask about the other girls' old schools, instead of performing tough stories every night.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to hear the stories every night?
qa.a: Charu feels uncomfortable and tired of the changing versions, so she quietly moves rooms without explaining.

grounding: It shows a teenager bragging about fights to gain status in a hostel while a roommate quietly distances herself, which the boaster notices only later.

passage:
Dear Deepika,
Guess what, I'm basically the most popular girl in Class 10 now. I told everyone about Papa's new car (the big one, not the old one) and how we're going to Dubai in December. Everyone was SO jealous. Then I told them how I shouted at that senior who pushed Tanu in the canteen, and she ran away. Well, she walked away, but fast.
Now everyone knows not to mess with me.
It's funny, though. Tanu and Riddhi have been eating lunch in the library this week. They say it's for studying. And when I told the Dubai story again on Friday, Riddhi kind of rolled her eyes? I think she's just jealous.
Anyway, write back and tell me if you have anything this exciting!
Love,
Madhuri

qa.q: Where did Madhuri say the family was going in December?
qa.a: To Dubai.

qa.q: Why does Madhuri keep telling the Dubai and canteen stories?
qa.a: Madhuri wants to feel important and ranked higher, and enjoys making others jealous, perhaps out of a need to be admired.

qa.q: What could Madhuri notice in her own letter?
qa.a: That Tanu and Riddhi are eating in the library and Riddhi rolled her eyes, signs the boasting is pushing friends away rather than impressing them.

qa.q: How might Riddhi be feeling when she hears the Dubai story again?
qa.a: Riddhi seems tired and irritated rather than jealous, which is why she rolled her eyes and has been eating elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a teenager boasting about money and a fight to rise in the group, while missing the signs that friends are quietly distancing.
